A vulnerability in the C2PA (Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity) specification allows for file content to be altered after signing without invalidating cryptographic signatures or Time Stamp Authority (TSA) timestamps. By leveraging the "exclusions" feature—which allows specific byte ranges to be omitted from signature calculations—a user can exclude the entire file and sign an empty string. The "exclusion" mechanism is a feature of the C2PA specification designed to accommodate file formats that require post-signature changes, such as updating CRC32 checksums in PNG files. Because current verification tools do not typically flag or restrict the size of these exclusion ranges, the technique allows for the creation of forged, timestamped media. A proposed mitigation involves requiring verifiers to enforce strict, format-specific constraints on which portions of a file are permitted to be excluded from a signature.

entry.title: Branch Target Reuse Attack Exploits Stale Branch Prediction in JIT Engines
entry.content:
Lobsters Top | vusec.net | discussion

Branch Target Reuse (BTR) is a Spectre-v2 attack that exploits stale indirect branch prediction entries in just-in-time (JIT) compilers. The vulnerability occurs when a CPU uses outdated branch targets from deallocated code to speculatively execute instructions in newly allocated code at the same memory address. This creates a speculative execute-after-free primitive that can bypass software hardening and facilitate control-flow hijacking in environments including the Linux kernel, Oracle GraalVM, and Firefox's SpiderMonkey engine.

entry.title: Comparing Typeclasses and Modules
entry.content:
Lobsters Top | sm2n.ca | discussion

Typeclasses provide ad-hoc polymorphism, enabling operator overloading and type-based dispatch to allow the same identifiers to be reused across different types. Modules provide modular abstraction through encapsulation, information hiding, and dependency injection, allowing for the recursive decomposition of programs into manageable components.

While these constructs can sometimes be used to emulate one another, they serve different architectural purposes: typeclasses facilitate "programming in the small" by managing localized logic, whereas modules facilitate "programming in the large" through high-level structural organization. The article examines how these mechanisms are implemented in languages such as Haskell, OCaml, Rust, and Elixir, arguing that robust modular abstraction is often more critical for software quality than ad-hoc polymorphism.
